title: The King Who Was So Rich He Crashed an Economy

youtube.title: The King Who Was So Rich He Crashed an Economy
youtube.description:
In 1324, Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire, traveled to Mecca and stopped in Cairo, where he spent and gave away so much gold that its value collapsed for years.
In this video, Sterling explains what happened, why it happened, and the simple economic rule behind it: inflation.
youtube.footer:
Sources: Ibn Fadlallah al-Umari, Masalik al-Absar (14th c.); the Catalan Atlas (1375).
This video is for education and entertainment, not financial advice.

#history #economics #money #mansamusa #inflation

scenes.say: In 1324, one man walked into Cairo with so much gold... that he accidentally crashed the economy.
His name was Mansa Musa... and he may have been the richest person who ever lived.
Hi, I'm Sterling, and today we're finding out how being too rich can actually break an economy.
Let's go back seven hundred years, to West Africa.
Mansa Musa ruled the Mali Empire, which stretched from the Atlantic coast far into the interior of West Africa.
And Mali had something the whole world wanted... gold. Lots and lots of gold.
Its mines were among the richest in the world, and Mali's gold flowed across the Sahara to North Africa, Europe and the Middle East.
So in 1324, when Mansa Musa set off on the pilgrimage to Mecca... he did not exactly pack light.
Chroniclers described an enormous caravan, by some accounts tens of thousands of people, and camels loaded with gold.
When he reached Cairo, Mansa Musa did what any extremely generous billionaire would do.
He spent gold. He gave gold away. To officials, to the poor, to pretty much everyone he met.
[whispers] And that's when things started to go wrong.
Suddenly, Cairo was flooded with gold.
And here's the rule that runs every economy on Earth: when something becomes common, it becomes less valuable.
If everyone has gold, gold stops being special. So merchants started asking for more of it, for the exact same things.
Prices went up. Each piece of gold bought less. Economists have a name for this: inflation.
And it didn't bounce back quickly. The historian al-Umari, writing about twelve years later, reported that gold in Cairo still hadn't recovered its value.
[laughs] One man's shopping trip shook the gold market of an entire region.
His fame spread all the way to Europe. On a famous map from 1375, the Catalan Atlas, Mansa Musa is drawn on a throne, holding a golden nugget.
But Mansa Musa wasn't just a big spender. Back home, he built mosques, and helped make Timbuktu a famous center of learning.
So what's the lesson here? Money is only valuable because it's scarce.
Flood the market with gold, or print too much money, and every coin buys a little less.
That's exactly what happened in Germany in 1923, and in Zimbabwe in 2008. But those are stories for another video.
If you want to know how money really works, subscribe. And tell me in the comments: what money mystery should I solve next?
